# stepFMR

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/jacksonmitch/stepFMR/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jacksonmitch/stepFMR/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

Finite Mixture Regression models allows relationships between the response ($\mathbf{Y}$) and the covariates $(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots, \mathbf{X}_p)$ to differ between a finite number of subpopulations. The R package, stepFMR implements stepwise procedures that select covariates having an effect on the response and determines whether each of the selected covariates has homogeneous or heterogeneous effects. The stepwise procedures are based on hypothesis testing where a weighted significance test (WEST) is used. In mixture regression, 
the unknown number of the subpopulations $G$ (referred as order of the mixture), poses challenges in testing the association between a covariate and the 
response. With WEST, the significance of a covariate's effects on $y$ is the weighted sum of the significance level of all candidate $G$'s. The package supports the Gaussian, Poisson, and Binomial distribution families, and returns the effect types of each covariate, estimate of their effects, as well as the best-fitting $G$.

## Installation

You can install the development version of stepFMR from
[GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("jacksonmitch/stepFMR")
```

## Example

This example simulates data from a two-component mixture where the true
answer is known, runs the stepwise WEST procedure, and then fits a model with
a specified structure. The vignette (`vignette("stepFMR")`) explains each step
in more detail.

### 1. Data generation

`simulate_fmr()` creates data from a mixture regression with coefficients that
you choose, so the fitted results can be checked against the truth. Each row of
`betas` holds the coefficients of one component, with columns for the
intercept and each covariate. Here the first covariate, `x1`, is heterogeneous, `x2` is homogeneous, and `x3` has no effect. `pi` is the mixing proportions of each component and `sigma` is the group specific standard deviations.

```{r simulate}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(stepFMR))

betas <- rbind(
  c(-2, -3, 1, 0),
  c(2, 3, 1, 0)
)
colnames(betas) <- c("(Intercept)", "x1", "x2", "x3")

sim <- simulate_fmr(
  n = 1000, betas = betas, pi = c(0.3, 0.7), sigma = c(0.5, 0.25),
  family = "gaussian", seed = 1
)
```

The result is a list. `sim$data` is a data frame with the response `y` and the
covariates `x1`, `x2` and `x3`. `sim$formula` is the model formula
`y ~ x1 + x2 + x3`, which names the response on the left and the covariates on
the right, just as in `lm()`. `sim$true_group` records which component each
observation came from. With your own data, pass your own formula and data frame
instead, for example `stepFMR(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = my_data)`.

### 2. WEST procedure

The number of components $G$ is unknown, and whether a covariate matters can
depend on it. `stepFMR()` therefore tests each covariate under every number of
components from 2 to `G_max` and combines the results into one weighted
p-value (WEST). It runs in two stages. Variable selection decides which
covariates have an effect. Effect determination then decides whether each
selected covariate is heterogeneous or homogeneous. `G_max = 3` means
that models with 2 and 3 components are compared, and the one with the lowest
BIC is reported.

```{r west}
fit <- stepFMR(sim$formula, sim$data, G_max = 3)
print(fit)
```

The printed result lists the selected covariates, how each effect was
classified, and the estimates at the best number of components. To see the WEST 
procedure, `print_steps()` shows the weighted p-value of every candidate at each step. 
A candidate is added when its p-value is below `alpha` (0.05 by default).

```{r steps}
print_steps(fit$variable_selection)
print_steps(fit$effect_determination)
```

### 3. Fitting

If you already know which covariates have a common effect, `fitFMR()` fits that
structure directly, without the stepwise search. `common = "x2"` makes `x2`
homogeneous, and `G_max = 3` compares models with 2 and 3 components by BIC.

```{r fit}
fit_fixed <- fitFMR(sim$formula, sim$data, G_max = 3, common = "x2")
fit_fixed
```

Mixture components have no natural order, so the fitted components can be
numbered differently from the simulated ones. Because the true groups are
known here, `match_groups()` relabels the fit to agree with them. The rows of
the matrix below can then be compared directly with the rows of `betas`.

```{r match}
aligned <- match_groups(fit, sim$true_group)
aligned$best_fit$parameter_values[["beta_g"]]
```

### Other families

The package supports `family = "poisson"` and `family = "binomial"`. For binomial data
the response is `cbind(successes, failures)`, which `simulate_fmr()` builds for 
you from the number of trials given by `size`.

```{r poisson}
sim_pois <- simulate_fmr(
  n = 500,
  betas = rbind(c(-0.5, -1, 0.3, 0), c(0.5, 1, 0.3, 0)),
  pi = c(0.4, 0.6), family = "poisson", seed = 2
)
fit_pois <- stepFMR(sim_pois$formula, sim_pois$data, G_max = 3, family = "poisson")
print(fit_pois)
```

```{r binomial}
sim_bin <- simulate_fmr(
  n = 500,
  betas = rbind(c(-1, -3, 0.5, 0), c(1, 3, 0.5, 0)),
  pi = c(0.4, 0.6), family = "binomial", size = 25, seed = 3
)
fit_bin <- stepFMR(sim_bin$formula, sim_bin$data, G_max = 3, family = "binomial")
print(fit_bin)
```
